pedagogy.summary: Children extend coordinate work to the full plane: plotting and reading points such as (−3,4) and (2,−5) across all four quadrants, naming which quadrant a point lies in, and describing positions where either or both coordinates are negative. The new demand is not the (across, up) convention itself — that carries over from the first quadrant — but reading a SIGNED scale on each axis: a negative x means left of the origin, a negative y means below it, and the numbers run symmetrically outward from 0 in both directions. Success rests on secure directed-number sense fused to the ordered-pair rule.
bestPractices: Anchor both axes as signed number lines meeting at the origin: rehearse pointing and chanting positive and negative values on a counting stick held horizontally (x) and vertically (y), forwards and backwards, so left/below map to negatives (NCETM).
Emphasise the symmetry about 0 — the numbers mirror outward from the origin — so children read −3 as three to the LEFT, not three to the right.
Keep the reading rule explicit and mnemonic — 'along the corridor and up (or down) the stairs', 'x is a-cross', 'x before y' — to hold off the perennial y-before-x reversal (NCETM).
Always plot the first coordinate along x from the origin THEN the second along y, treating each sign as a direction, not a decoration on the digit.
Name the four quadrants by the sign pattern of their points (+,+), (−,+), (−,−), (+,−) so 'which quadrant?' becomes a reading of the two signs, and connect this to reflections in the axes.
Use problems that force reasoning across quadrants (find the fourth vertex of a square given (3,0), (0,3), (−3,0)) rather than isolated plotting, so signs must be coordinated.
keyRepresentations: Four-quadrant coordinate grid with the origin and both signed axes labelled
Counting stick / number line held horizontally and vertically to model signed movement along each axis
Thermometer or below-ground scale as a familiar signed vertical axis
Sign-pattern labels for the four quadrants: (+,+), (−,+), (−,−), (+,−)
commonMisconceptions: Moving the wrong way for a negative coordinate — counting right for −3 or up for −5 — through weak grasp of order on a signed scale.
Putting the y-coordinate before the x-coordinate, placing the point in the wrong quadrant.
Mis-ordering negatives (treating −5 as further out than −3 because 5>3), so points on a negative axis are misplaced.
Counting from '1' at the origin instead of '0', landing one square off.

learn.summary: Children extend coordinate work to all four quadrants: plotting and reading points such as (−3,4) and (2,−5), naming which quadrant a point lies in, and reasoning about positions where either or both coordinates are negative. The new demand is reading a SIGNED scale on each axis — a negative x means left of the origin, a negative y means below it, with numbers running symmetrically outward from 0 — fused to the ordered-pair (across, then up/down) rule. Live plotting with immediate feedback lets wrong-direction and reversed placements surface and be corrected; discrete practice items and labelled grids can check and clarify but elicit less of the felt signed movement.

activities.title: Plot it as a signed journey from the origin
feedback: If (−3,4) lands in the top-right (first) quadrant, the x-move went the wrong way: count the negative as LEFT from 0 and re-plot.
If the point lands as if it were (4,−3), the pair was reversed — move along x first ('along the corridor, then up or down the stairs').
Linked feedback that lights each axis's signed count as the marker travels makes the two moves and the landing quadrant visible together.
Reflecting (−3,4) in the x-axis gives (−3,−4) — the y-sign flips and the point drops to the third quadrant; check which single sign changed.
activities.rationale: Plotting on a signed grid is direct manipulation: the child performs two signed movements and can see a wrong direction or a reversed pair immediately, which is where signed-coordinate errors surface. Reading the quadrant from the sign pattern and linking sign flips to reflection connects the skill to geometry the child already knows.
sourceClaims: Year 6 pupils should describe positions on the full coordinate grid (all four quadrants), including with negative numbers.

Recommended teaching includes mnemonics ('along the corridor and up the stairs', 'x is a-cross', 'x before y'), chanting positive and negative numbers on a counting stick held both horizontally and vertically for the two axes, and referring to the symmetry of the numbers about 0.
learnerActions: On a four-quadrant grid with a labelled origin and signed axes, plot (−3,4): move LEFT 3 along the x-axis from the origin, then UP 4 along the y-axis, treating each sign as a direction.
Name the quadrant from its sign pattern: (−,+) is the second (top-left) quadrant.
Plot (2,−5) (two right, five down) and (−4,−1) (four left, one down), naming each quadrant from its two signs.

If a live tool is available, place the marker yourself and watch it replay the two signed moves; if you counted right for the −3 and landed in the (+,+) quadrant, notice the mismatch and re-plot reading the minus as 'left'.
Where offered, use a reflect-in-axis toggle to flip (−3,4)↔(3,4)↔(3,−4) and watch a single sign change hop the point across an axis.
activities.intendedInsight: A minus sign is a DIRECTION (left of, or below, the origin), not decoration on the digit; the quadrant is read directly from the pair of signs, and flipping one sign reflects the point across an axis.

activities.title: Anchor each axis as a signed number line
feedback: If the child taps the origin while saying 'one', re-establish the origin as 0 and count moves from there; otherwise every point lands one square off.
If −5 is placed nearer the origin than −3 because 5>3, count steps out from 0 on the line: −5 is five steps out, −3 is three.
A counting stick or washing-line chanted in both directions makes the symmetry about 0 audible and visible.
activities.rationale: Secure directed-number sense underpins signed plotting; ordering negatives is genuinely hard because children treat magnitude as value, and number-line / thermometer / depth models address this by foregrounding position on the scale.
sourceClaims: Children find ordering negative integers difficult — numbers less than zero represent 'the non-existent' and the idea that 0 is greater than −1 is hard; the underlying error is treating the magnitude/digit as the value rather than the position on the scale, best addressed with number-line, washing-line, thermometer and swimming-pool (depth) models.

Recommended teaching includes mnemonics ('along the corridor and up the stairs', 'x is a-cross', 'x before y'), chanting positive and negative numbers on a counting stick held both horizontally and vertically for the two axes, and referring to the symmetry of the numbers about 0.
learnerActions: Treat the x-axis as a horizontal number line and the y-axis as a vertical one, both meeting at 0 at the origin.
Point and chant positive and negative values along a counting stick held horizontally, then vertically, forwards and backwards, so left and below map to negatives.
Use a thermometer or below-ground/depth scale as a familiar signed vertical axis.
Count the MOVES from the origin (which is 0), not the lines including it, so you do not land one square off.
Say aloud why −3 goes three to the LEFT: the numbers mirror symmetrically outward from 0.
activities.intendedInsight: Each axis is a signed number line symmetric about 0; reading position (not the bare digit) on that scale is what fixes direction and ordering.

activities.title: Reason across quadrants and name the quadrant from the signs
feedback: If a quadrant is named by memorised position rather than sign pattern, re-read the two signs: (−,−) is the third (bottom-left) quadrant.
If the child says (−3,0) is further from the origin than (−5,0), count steps from 0 along the negative axis.
For the square, use the symmetry about the origin: the vertex opposite (0,3) completes it, so the fourth vertex is (0,−3).
activities.rationale: Problems that force coordination of signs across quadrants, and distinguishing distance-from-0 from the digit, reveal whether the child reads signs as direction and can transfer to unplotted points rather than reaching a square by rote.
sourceClaims: For the Year 6 objective 'read and plot coordinates in all four quadrants', two named misconceptions are putting the y-coordinate before the x-coordinate, and misplaced positions due to a lack of understanding of the order of negative numbers on a scale.
Year 6 pupils should describe positions on the full coordinate grid (all four quadrants), including with negative numbers.
learnerActions: Without plotting, state which quadrant (−2,−7) lies in and explain how you can tell from the two signs.
Find the fourth vertex of a square given three vertices such as (3,0), (0,3), (−3,0), coordinating the signs rather than plotting in isolation.
Compare (−5,0) and (−3,0): decide which is further from the origin and justify it by position on the negative scale (five to the left versus three).
Label each quadrant by its sign pattern: (+,+), (−,+), (−,−), (+,−), and connect this to reflections in the axes.
Respond to a counterexample: 'A friend plotted (−3,4) in the top-right — what would you say?' (a negative x must go left).
activities.intendedInsight: For a point with two non-zero coordinates, quadrant membership is a reading of the two signs; a point with a zero coordinate, such as (3,0), (0,3) or (−5,0), lies on an axis and is in no quadrant. Coordinating signs across quadrants and comparing negatives by distance from the origin transfers the skill beyond single plots.

activities.title: Check and diagnose with targeted items
feedback: Picking the sign-flipped option signals a sign was read as decoration; return to reading the minus as direction.
Picking the reversed-pair option signals y-before-x; re-anchor 'x before y'.
activities.rationale: Well-designed items assess cleanly and the pattern of wrong options chosen can pinpoint the misconception, but recognition and single-step plotting elicit less independent, felt signed movement than live plotting, so they complement rather than replace it.
sourceClaims: For the Year 6 objective 'read and plot coordinates in all four quadrants', two named misconceptions are putting the y-coordinate before the x-coordinate, and misplaced positions due to a lack of understanding of the order of negative numbers on a scale.
learnerActions: Tap/draw to plot (−3,4); choose which quadrant (2,−5) is in; fill in the coordinates of a plotted point; put −5, −3, 0, 2 in order along an axis.

For multiple-choice quadrant questions, the wrong options should encode real errors — the reversed point, the same point with one sign flipped, and the point mis-ordered on the negative scale — so a wrong answer shows which misconception is present.
activities.intendedInsight: Discrete items confirm the skill and diagnose which specific error (reversal, sign-as-decoration, or mis-ordered negatives) is present.

constraints: The (across, then up/down) ordering convention carries over from the first quadrant; the genuinely new demand is reading the SIGNED scale on each axis, so secure directed-number sense is a prerequisite.
Recognition-only practice items confirm and diagnose but do not by themselves elicit independent construction of the two signed movements; pair them with actual plotting where possible.

A static labelled four-quadrant grid can reveal a point's signed path and each quadrant's sign pattern on tap, which clarifies layout, but it does not let the child plot and self-check, which is where signed errors surface — treat it as a scaffold.
Keep to the 2D plane for this objective; introducing a third axis brings octants and z-values beyond this topic and would obscure the signed 2D reading.
Reflect-in-axis toggles, axis-lighting counts, and live replay are optional feedback examples that make the mechanism concrete; they are not mandatory.
Always count MOVES from the origin (0), not the grid lines including it, to avoid the one-square-off error.
reviewNotes: This is an agent semantic rewrite of saved teaching research without fresh source verification; sources were not re-fetched. Activities are research-informed proposals, not validated interventions.

The square example (vertices (3,0), (0,3), (−3,0)) has fourth vertex (0,−3) if the intended figure is a square centred on the origin (verified: right angle at (0,3), diagonal length 6); confirm the intended shape before use, as other three-point arrangements could complete different quadrilaterals.
One cited claim (National Curriculum, all-four-quadrants with negatives) is marked verified:false in the source row; treat its evidential weight accordingly.

The original source framed the live-plotting tool as uniquely building fluency and a conversation/3D as unable to teach this; softened to scoped affordances/limits without asserting comparative efficacy, which the exact sources do not establish.

probeDeeper: Point at (2,−5): 'How did you know to go down rather than up for the −5?' (listen for the sign read as direction, not a rule recited).
'Which quadrant would (−2, −7) be in, without plotting it? How can you tell?' (tests reading the quadrant from the two signs alone).
Counterexample: 'A friend plotted (−3,4) up here in the top-right. What would you say to them?' (elicits that a negative x must go left, exposing the sign-as-decoration error).
'If you reflect (−3,4) in the x-axis, what are the new coordinates and which quadrant is it in now?' (links sign change to reflection across an axis).
assess.correctAnswer: The child moves along x first then y, treating each sign as a direction — (−3,4) three left and four up (second quadrant), (2,−5) two right and five down (fourth quadrant), (−4,−1) four left and one down (third quadrant) — labels each pair as (across, up), names the quadrant from the sign pattern, and reasons that (−5,0) is further from the origin than (−3,0) because −5 is further along the negative scale (five to the left versus three).

errorPatterns.pattern: Moves the wrong way for a negative coordinate — counts right for −3 or up for −5 — treating the minus as decoration rather than a direction
errorPatterns.nextMove: Rehearse the axis as a signed number line with a counting stick — negatives go left/down from 0, symmetric about the origin; re-plot reading the sign as the direction.
errorPatterns.revealedBy: (−3,4) lands in the first quadrant instead of the second; the child counts away from 0 in the positive direction regardless of sign.

errorPatterns.pattern: Puts the y-coordinate before the x-coordinate, so the point lands in the wrong place
errorPatterns.nextMove: Re-anchor 'along the corridor, then up/down the stairs', 'x before y'; check one point together, moving x first.
errorPatterns.revealedBy: (−3,4) plotted as if (4,−3) — wrong quadrant — though the child clearly used both numbers; often surfaces as a swapped quadrant.

errorPatterns.pattern: Mis-orders negatives, treating −5 as nearer the origin than −3 (or vice versa) because 5>3 — magnitude read as value
errorPatterns.nextMove: Use a number line / thermometer through 0: count steps from the origin, showing −5 is five steps out and −3 is three; contrast distance-from-0 with the digit.
errorPatterns.revealedBy: Says (−3,0) is further from the origin than (−5,0), or spaces negative points as if −5 sits between 0 and −3.

errorPatterns.pattern: Counts from '1' at the origin rather than '0', landing one square short or long
errorPatterns.nextMove: Establish the origin as 0; count the MOVES from the origin, not the lines including it; re-plot one point together.
errorPatterns.revealedBy: Every plotted point is consistently one square off along an axis; the child taps the origin as they say 'one'.

responseLevels.gap: Cannot reliably place signed points — ignores signs or reverses the pair, so points land in the wrong quadrants — and cannot compare negatives on a scale (thinks −3 is further out than −5).
responseLevels.full: Plots points in all four quadrants by reading each sign as a direction (x then y), labels them (across, up), names each quadrant from its sign pattern, orders negatives correctly by distance from the origin, and transfers — e.g. states a point's quadrant without plotting and predicts the effect of reflecting it in an axis.
responseLevels.partial: Plots first-quadrant and single-negative points but falters when both coordinates are negative or when asked to justify — e.g. reaches the right square by rule yet cannot explain WHY −3 goes left, or names quadrants by memorised position rather than by sign pattern, and mis-orders negatives on the scale. Executes the steps but cannot connect sign to direction or transfer to an unplotted point.

assess.diagnosticPrompt: Put a four-quadrant grid with a labelled origin and signed axes in front of the child. Say: 'Plot these three points and label each with its coordinates: (−3, 4), (2, −5), and (−4, −1). For each one, tell me which quadrant it is in. Then look at (−5, 0) and (−3, 0) — which is further from the origin, and how do you know?' Set the task and WATCH how each point is reached from the origin; do not explain the axes.
assess.whatMakesItDiscriminate: Points with mixed signs give a DIFFERENT landing quadrant for a child who reads signs as directions than for one who ignores the sign, reverses the pair, or mis-orders negatives — each error sends the point to a distinct, visible wrong place. Watching the origin-to-point movement (which axis first, which direction) reveals the reasoning directly, and the (−5,0) vs (−3,0) question isolates negative-scale ordering from the plotting itself.
